strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful question: how adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while achieving low robust training error and poor robust test performance.
The distinction between learning shared signal and memorizing instance-specific noise offers an interpretable candidate mechanism. The proposed three-stage dynamics makes this explanation concrete.

The experiments include MNIST/CIFAR10 width sweeps, synthetic feature trajectories, and input-flatness measurements. Table 1 illustrates the motivating phenomenon, including 86.05% clean test accuracy versus 50.08% robust test accuracy on CIFAR10.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. A distribution supported on two well-separated points satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3: a small ReLU classifier can classify both points correctly while failing nearby. With polynomially growing sample size, both points have empirical frequencies approaching one-half. Vanishing robust training error then forces zero robust population error, excluding CGRO. A distributional condition limiting training-neighborhood coverage is missing. Appendix F also incorrectly claims uniform arbitrarily accurate approximation of the generally discontinuous construction f_S by continuous ReLU networks.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robustness under the threat model in Definition 3.3. Section 5 permits perturbations only along the signal direction in the informative patch, leaving every noise patch unchanged. Convergence of this restricted adversarial loss does not imply low training error against the full norm ball. Appendix E.12 nevertheless makes that inference. This matters directly because the proposed memorization mechanism depends on noise that the training adversary cannot alter.

The dynamics proof has additional substantive gaps. Assumption 5.7 permits c_alpha > 1/2, for which the stated Gaussian initialization already violates the uniform signal bound of order alpha^(-1), up to logarithmic factors, required by Hypothesis E.1 and Lemma E.11. Appendix E.12 also treats a cubic Gaussian polynomial as sub-Gaussian and applies an invalid tail bound; different filters share the same test noise and are correlated. These issues undermine the clean-generalization guarantee.

The additional generalization bound in Theorem B.1 is invalid as stated. A constant predictor has zero input-gradient term, yet random class proportions can produce a positive population-minus-empirical loss gap with nonvanishing probability. The bound therefore requires a sampling term or additional restrictions. Appendix G does not resolve this counterexample.

The synthetic experiment uses delta = alpha = 10, contradicting Assumption 5.7's strict delta < alpha while being described as satisfying that assumption. At this radius, the adversary can erase the only informative patch, leaving label-independent noise; robust error of at least one-half is then unavoidable for any classifier. This experiment cannot validate the claimed mechanism in the theorem's regime.

The novelty and explanatory reach of the representation lower bound need clarification. As described in the manuscript, Li et al. (2022) already establishes an exponential lower bound for a linearly separable construction. Such distributions also admit polynomial-size clean classifiers, so broadening the admissible class does not itself strengthen the existential statement of Theorem 4.7. Furthermore, a worst-case construction does not establish the proposed capacity explanation for the image datasets.

The empirical evaluation provides limited support for the causal interpretation and insufficient reproducibility detail. CIFAR10 robust train–test gaps are 20.80, 36.08, 51.12, and 49.49 percentage points across increasing widths, showing only a small decrease at the largest width. Input-flatness correlations do not establish local memorization as the cause. PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, several training settings, and variability across seeds are unreported. These experiments cannot compensate for the unresolved correctness issues in the principal theorems.
